title: Urinary Bladder & Urethra Anatomy
descriptor: Location, Wall & Trigone, Sphincters, Storage & Voiding, Infection & Incontinence
intro: The urinary bladder is a muscular organ in the pelvis that stores the urine sent down from the kidneys through the ureters. To empty it, the brain signals the sphincters to relax and the muscular wall to tighten, so that urine is pushed out through the urethra. Between emptyings the sphincter muscles stay contracted and keep the urethra closed. The urethra arises from the base of the bladder and carries urine out of the body.

keyFacts.label: Location
keyFacts.value: Lesser pelvis behind the pubic symphysis in adults, rising into the abdomen as it fills

keyFacts.label: Wall
keyFacts.value: Urothelial lining, lamina propria, detrusor smooth muscle and an outer serosa or adventitia

keyFacts.label: Trigone
keyFacts.value: Smooth triangle at the base formed by the two ureteric openings and the urethral opening; richest in sensory nerve receptors

keyFacts.label: Sphincters
keyFacts.value: Involuntary internal sphincter of smooth muscle and voluntary external sphincter of skeletal muscle

keyFacts.label: Arteries
keyFacts.value: Superior and inferior vesical arteries, branches of the internal iliac arteries

keyFacts.label: Lymph drainage
keyFacts.value: Mostly to the external iliac nodes

keyFacts.label: Investigation
keyFacts.value: Cystoscopy, a thin camera tube passed through the urethra into the bladder

sections.heading: Location and relations
sections.body: In adults the bladder lies in the lesser pelvis when it is empty, directly behind the pubic symphysis, and rises into the abdomen as it fills. It is described as having four parts: the apex or dome, the body, the fundus or base, and the neck. Peritoneum covers the upper surface of the bladder. Where a prostate is present, the base of the bladder is firmly attached to the prostate and the rectum lies behind. Where a vagina is present, the base of the bladder and the urethra rest on its anterior wall. The muscles of the pelvic floor support the bladder from below. Surgeons must identify the bladder during caesarean section to avoid injuring it.

sections.heading: Wall, lining and trigone
sections.body: The bladder wall has four layers: an inner urothelial lining, a lamina propria of connective tissue containing blood vessels and nerve endings, the detrusor muscle, and an outer serosa or adventitia. The urothelium is thick when the bladder is relaxed and thins as the bladder fills, without structural damage. The detrusor is made of crisscrossing bands of smooth muscle, with fibres arranged in spiral, longitudinal and circular bundles, and the whole organ is highly distensible. On the inner surface the trigone is a smooth triangular area formed by the two ureteric openings and the opening of the urethra. It has the highest concentration of sensory nerve receptors in the bladder. The trigone and the bladder neck are more firmly anchored to the tissue beneath and do not shrink as much during emptying or form rugae.

sections.heading: Urethra and sphincters
sections.body: The urethra begins at the trigone area at the base of the bladder. The male urethra also carries semen and is described in four regions: the preprostatic, prostatic, membranous and spongy or penile urethra. Two sphincters control the outflow of urine, and contracting them narrows the urethra to slow or stop urination. The internal sphincter is smooth muscle, continuous with the detrusor, and works involuntarily; in the male urethra it also helps stop semen flowing back into the bladder during ejaculation. The external sphincter is skeletal muscle under voluntary control and is supplied by the pudendal nerve. Problems with the sphincters are commonly linked to urinary incontinence.

sections.heading: Blood supply, nerves and lymph
sections.body: The superior and inferior vesical arteries, branches of the internal iliac arteries, are the main arterial supply, with the superior vesical artery feeding the upper bladder. Venous blood drains through the vesical venous plexus into the internal iliac veins, and lymph drains mostly to the external iliac nodes. Sympathetic and parasympathetic nerves arising from the pelvic plexus supply the bladder, together with somatic fibres. Sympathetic activity, through the hypogastric nerves, suppresses contraction of the detrusor, whereas parasympathetic activity contracts the detrusor and relaxes the internal sphincter. Sensation from the upper wall travels with sympathetic fibres, and sensation from the lower wall with parasympathetic fibres.

sections.heading: Storage and voiding
sections.body: The bladder acts as both a storage reservoir and an excretory organ. Urination alternates between a storage phase, when urine collects, and a voiding phase, when the bladder empties. During storage the detrusor stays relaxed as the bladder fills, while the sphincter muscles stay contracted to keep urine in. Continuous sympathetic tone through the hypogastric nerve keeps the detrusor relaxed, and the pudendal nerve closes the external sphincter to support continence. Voiding starts when strong sensory signals from the bladder activate reflex pathways in the brainstem, including the pontine micturition centre, also known as Barrington's nucleus, which coordinates emptying. The detrusor then contracts, the sphincters relax and urine flows out through the urethra.

sections.heading: Infection and bladder pain
sections.body: Cystitis is a urinary tract infection that affects the bladder. It often gets better by itself, but may sometimes be treated with antibiotics. Symptoms include pain or burning when passing urine, needing to go more often and urgently, dark, cloudy or strong-smelling urine, and pain low in the tummy. The shorter female urethra is linked to a higher incidence of bladder infections. A more severe infection can cause pain in the back or side, particularly under the ribs, in the area of the kidneys. The NHS says cystitis symptoms in children, and in people with a prostate, should always be assessed by a clinician. Bladder pain syndrome, or interstitial cystitis, is a chronic condition in which pain usually worsens as the bladder fills and eases after urinating; severity ranges from mild discomfort to intense pain.

sections.heading: Incontinence and bladder cancer
sections.body: The NHS describes several types of urinary incontinence. In stress incontinence urine leaks when the bladder is put under sudden extra pressure, for example by coughing, sneezing or heavy lifting. Urge incontinence is leakage linked to a sudden, strong need to pass urine and often occurs with overactive bladder syndrome, in which the bladder muscle is more active than usual. Most bladder cancers begin in the urothelial cells that line the urinary tract. Blood in the urine is the commonest warning sign; it may look pink, red or dark brown, may come and go, or may show up only on a laboratory test. It is usually caused by something other than cancer, such as infection or stones, but the NHS advises that it should be assessed by a clinician even when there are no other symptoms.

sections.heading: How the bladder is investigated
sections.body: Cystoscopy lets a clinician look at the lining of the bladder. A thin tube with a camera is gently passed into the urethra and moved through it into the bladder. Saline is run into the bladder to inflate it, which makes it easier to see inside, and local anaesthetic gel numbs the urethra beforehand. The ureteric openings can also be seen at cystoscopy. For suspected bladder cancer the NCI describes starting with a urine sample, with cystoscopy and imaging ordered if needed, and diagnosis and staging usually begin with cystoscopy.
